draft:
The most revealing thing in **MILLION DOLLAR BABY** is the bit in parentheses. "Cause I wanna make it (so badly)," Tommy Richman sings, then answers the boast before anyone else can: "I'm a Million Dollar Baby (don't at me)." That small aside carries the whole song. It's a big claim with a flinch built into it. The narrator names their own worth and in the same breath expects to be laughed at for it.

Everything around that hook is a case being argued. The chorus opens with a defense nobody asked for: never repped a set, never did wrong, could clean up good for you, knows right from wrong. It reads like someone rehearsing for an interview they're afraid they'll fail. Underneath the swagger is a plea to be seen as safe, decent, worth the bet. Then the grievance comes out plainly. The city has been repped for so long by somebody else, and the narrator still goes unnoticed. "VA next," "My sound next" isn't only bragging. It's the voice of someone tired of waiting their turn and claiming home ground out loud so it can't be ignored.

The love story running through the verse knots the same feelings together. There's a woman, a rival who can't come between them again, a night spent showing her off to friends that didn't lift the mood. Then the line that gives the narrator away: "What you mean I changed." The next words insist they haven't stayed the same, and right after that comes the admission of losing their mind. Pride and unraveling sit side by side, and the song never sorts them out. The song closes on three flat refusals, a door slammed on the accusation of change without ever answering it.

The music makes all that ambition sound easy, which is part of the trick. A synth bass works a simple, repeating line while a high, percussive synth picks out a counter-melody on top. Kick and snare keep a steady, moderate pace, and the groove sits back with a slight swing, never pushing. Richman's delivery runs between rhythm and melody, half-spoken and loose, with no harmonies stacked behind it. The room is dry and the mix is clean, so every part sits in its own lane and that lone voice stays right up front. There's no crowd behind the narrator, just one person making a case.

The release came out in 2024 on ISO Supremacy, licensed to PULSE Records, and it moves fast.

It sticks because the swagger keeps showing its seams, and you end up rooting for someone who wants it so badly they have to tell you not to laugh.

factCheck.claim: "Cause I wanna make it (so badly)" and "I'm a Million Dollar Baby (don't at me)" are quoted lines
factCheck.note: Both match the lyrics exactly and are consecutive lines, so they count as the two-line limit.
Tommy Richman is the credited artist.
The draft quoted five separate lyric lines, over the three-line cap. These two were turned into a paraphrase. They also appeared in reverse order from the lyrics.
Matches the lyrics exactly. Kept as the third and last quoted line.

factCheck.claim: The chorus opens with never repping a set, never doing wrong, cleaning up good, knowing right from wrong
factCheck.note: Matches the repeated opening lines of the lyrics.

factCheck.claim: The city has been repped for so long by somebody else, and the narrator still goes unnoticed
factCheck.note: The lyric addresses 'you' who reps the city for so long and still doesn't notice the narrator. Reworded to match.

factCheck.claim: A rival who can't come between them again
factCheck.note: Based on 'he cannot come between us again'. The reading is interpretive but rests on the lyric.

factCheck.claim: A night spent showing her off to friends that didn't lift the mood
factCheck.note: The lyric says she was taken to Queen's Gambit and shown around, but never says it was a night. Changed to 'an outing'.

factCheck.claim: The next words insist they haven't stayed the same, then the admission of losing their mind
factCheck.note: Order is right, but 'Haven't stayed the same' is ambiguous. Reworded so it isn't presented as an insistence.

factCheck.claim: The song closes on three flat refusals
factCheck.note: The lyrics end with three repeats of 'Hell no'. The reading about the accusation of change is kept as interpretation.
